title: Attention Is All You Need, explained: How Transformer built the foundation for every large model
summary: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all run on the Transformer under the hood. The 2017 paper threw out recurrent networks and processed language with attention alone. We unpack the problem, the formulas, and the experiments piece by piece, with worked examples and self-check questions, so that by the end you can explain why it works.
ai_summary: In 2017, researchers at Google introduced the Transformer at NIPS: instead of processing sentences word by word in order, every word attends to the whole sentence at once. Its core is scaled dot-product attention (divided by √dₖ to prevent softmax saturation), 8-head multi-head attention, sinusoidal positional encoding, and a stack of 6 encoder layers and 6 decoder layers. It reached 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, more than 2 points above the previous best, training on 8 GPUs for 3.5 days. Limits: compute grows quadratically with sequence length, generation is still word by word; English-to-French is reported as 41.8 in the abstract and 41.0 in the body.
brief: The problem: recurrent networks must compute one word at a time, cannot be parallelized, and distant words have to pass information through many intermediate steps.

The method: attention only. Each word uses a query to match all words' keys, and retrieves their values by weight; eight heads each look in their own way, and sinusoidal positional encoding adds word order back.
The result: 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, more than 2 points above the best previous result including ensembles; the base model costs a fraction of the training cost of its rivals.
The impact: GPT, BERT, and today's large language models all build on this architecture; the quadratic compute problem it left behind is still an active research area.

paper.title: Attention Is All You Need
paper.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
paper.org: Google Brain · Google Research · University of Toronto

cover.headline: A close reading of the original Transformer paper
cover.highlight: Understanding a sentence with attention alone

sections.h: The bottom line: what the paper actually did

blocks.p: In 2017, eight researchers from Google Brain, Google Research, and the University of Toronto published this paper, just 10 pages long, at NIPS 2017. It proposed a neural network architecture called **Transformer**: when processing a sentence, instead of reading it one word at a time in order, it lets every word look at all the words in the sentence at once, then decide which ones to draw on and how much. That mechanism of deciding who to look at and how much is called **attention**.

The paper set out to solve a concrete problem: machine translation. It delivered concrete results: 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, more than 2 points above the previous best, including ensembles; the largest model trained in 3.5 days on a single machine with eight P100 GPUs.

But its impact went far beyond translation. Today's ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all Transformer variants underneath; the T in GPT stands for Transformer. So reading this paper is a key to understanding all large models. Below, we start with the problem it set out to solve, take the pieces apart one by one, then put them back together.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: Transformer = attention (each word looks at the whole sentence and takes information by relevance) + feed-forward network (each word is processed in place) + positional encoding (adds word order) + residual connections and layer normalization (makes deep stacks trainable). Stack this layer six times.

callout.title: Three small concepts to know first
callout.text: No background required; these three are enough:
list: **Vector**: a list of numbers. The model represents a word's meaning as a list of numbers; words with similar meanings have similar numbers.

**Dot product**: multiply two lists of numbers position by position and add the results. The more the two vectors point in the same direction, the larger the dot product—roughly speaking, the more similar they are.
**softmax**: turns a set of scores into proportions that add up to 1; the higher the score, the larger its share.

sections.h: Before it: why reading one word at a time hit a wall

blocks.p: Before 2017, the dominant translation models were **recurrent neural networks** (RNNs, and their improved variants LSTM and GRU). They read a sentence much like a person pointing at each word: at word t, the model holds a single memory hₜ computed from the previous memory hₜ₋₁ and the current word.

The paper identifies the fundamental problem: **you must finish the previous step before you can start the next**. There is no parallelism within a sentence, so longer sentences are slower; and as sentences grow, memory limits how many can be processed at once. A GPU is best at doing many identical computations at once, but an RNN makes it wait in line.

The second problem is that long-distance information has to travel by relay. For a subject at the start of a sentence to influence a verb at the end, the signal must pass through the memory of every word in between; the farther it travels, the more it degrades. The paper measures this with **path length**: in an RNN, a signal between two positions n words apart has to travel O(n) steps.

Some used convolutional networks for parallelism (the paper compares ConvS2S and ByteNet), but a single convolution only sees nearby words; connecting distant words requires stacking many layers. ConvS2S path length grows linearly with distance; ByteNet grows logarithmically.

Attention was proposed as early as 2014, but almost always as a plug-in for RNNs. This paper asks a bold question: what if we drop recurrence and convolution and keep **only attention**? The title, “Attention Is All You Need,” is its answer.

sections.h: What attention is: a weighted lookup

callout.title: Think of attention as a trip to the library
callout.text: You walk into the library with a question (the **query**). Each book has a label on its spine (the **key**), and inside is the actual content (the **value**). You compare your question with each label, and the books that match best get the most attention; the answer you get is the books' contents blended together according to how well they match. In a Transformer, every word in the sentence plays all three roles at once: the one asking, the label being compared, and the content being retrieved.

blocks.p: The paper defines attention in a single sentence: it maps a query and a set of key–value pairs to an output, where the output is a weighted sum of the values and each value's weight is determined by how well the query matches its key. The specific algorithm the paper uses is called **Scaled Dot-Product Attention**, written as:

formula.expr: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √dₖ ) · V

parts.desc: Query matrix: each row is what a word is looking for.
Key matrix: each row is the label for how a word can be found.
Value matrix: each row is the information a word actually carries.
Take the dot product of every query with every key to get a score table of how related each pair is.
The square root of the key vector dimension dₖ, used to shrink the scores; the next section explains why.
Turn each row of the score table into weights that add up to 1.
Use these weights to average the values and get a new representation for each word.

formula.note: The whole process is just two matrix multiplications and one softmax—exactly the kind of computation GPUs are best at—so a whole sentence can be computed at once.

blocks.p: Where do Q, K, and V come from? Each word is first represented as a 512-dimensional vector (d_{model} = 512 in the paper), then multiplied by three learnable matrices W^{Q}, W^{K}, and W^{V} to produce its query, key, and value. These three matrices are learned during training: the model figures out what each word should ask for, what label it should present, and what content it should hand over.

Let's work through a tiny example by hand. Suppose the sentence is “cat sat mat” (a three-token toy sentence), and we are computing attention for “cat,” with vector dimension dₖ = 4. The numbers are invented to keep the arithmetic easy.

fig.title: Worked attention example: “cat” attends most to itself, then to “mat”
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: vectors are invented for the example, not from the paper. Query q = [1, 0, 1, 0], dₖ = 4, so √dₖ = 2.
fig.note: Output = 0.506×[10, 0] + 0.186×[0, 10] + 0.307×[5, 5] ≈ [6.6, 3.4]. In the new representation of “cat,” its own information accounts for more than half, with a good amount of “mat” mixed in.

blocks.p: Notice two things. First, the weights are **relative**: softmax only cares about differences between scores, not their absolute size. Second, the output is a **blend**: the new vector for “cat” no longer just represents the word “cat,” but something like “the cat that sat on the mat in this sentence.” As layer after layer blends like this, each word's representation becomes more context-aware.

callout.title: Attention is not just highlighting a few words
callout.text: Many people imagine attention as highlighting the important words. It is actually a continuous weighted average: every word in the sentence is seen, just with larger or smaller weights; the weights are not hand-written rules but are learned from training data.

sections.h: Why divide by √dₖ: a crucial detail that is easy to skip

blocks.p: The √dₖ in the formula looks like a casually added constant, but the paper devotes a footnote to it, and it is key to understanding why attention trains at all.

The paper's derivation is as follows. Assume each component of query q and key k is an independent random variable with mean 0 and variance 1. Then their dot product q·k = q₁k₁ + q₂k₂ + … + q_{dₖ}k_{dₖ} is a sum of dₖ random variables, so it still has mean 0, but its **variance becomes dₖ**. In the paper each head has dₖ = 64, so the dot product's standard deviation is √64 = 8, and the scores routinely land in the teens or twenties.
When scores swing that much, softmax becomes extreme: the largest score takes nearly all the weight, and the rest approach 0. Look at this comparison:

fig.title: Same relative ratios, scores multiplied by 8: softmax gives almost all the weight to the top item
fig.subtitle: Illustrative calculation: the three scores have the same proportions; the second row is simply multiplied by 8.

blocks.p: When the weights are flattened into almost only 0 and 1, softmax sits in a region of **extremely small gradients**: however the model nudges its parameters, the output barely changes, so it receives no signal about how to adjust, and training stalls. Dividing by √dₖ pulls the dot-product variance back to 1, keeping softmax in the range where it can learn.

The paper also makes a comparison: another common form, “additive attention” (which computes match scores with a small neural network), outperforms **unscaled** dot-product attention when dₖ is large; once scaled, dot-product attention is both fast (it can use highly optimized matrix multiplication) and no longer at a disadvantage.

quiz.q: What happens if each head's dₖ grows from 64 to 256, but you still divide by 8 (i.e., keep scaling by √64)?
options: Dot-product variance becomes 4×, softmax becomes more extreme, gradients shrink, and training gets harder.
No effect; softmax only cares about relative scores.
Attention becomes more even, with similar weights for every word.
quiz.why: According to the paper's footnote derivation, the dot-product variance equals dₖ. Going from dₖ = 64 to 256 makes the variance 4 times larger, and the standard deviation rises from 8 to 16; dividing only by 8 still leaves scores twice as large as before, so softmax is more easily flattened. The correct change is to divide by √256 = 16. Option C is only half right: softmax does care only about relative size, but multiplying all scores up also magnifies the relative gaps.

sections.h: Multi-head attention: eight “experts,” each looking in its own way

blocks.p: A single attention head has a flaw: each word ends up as a weighted **average**, and averaging muddles different kinds of relationships together. Take the word “it”: it needs to know what it refers to (a coreference relation) and what role it plays in the sentence (a syntactic relation), and a single average has trouble carrying both at once. The paper's own words: with only one head, averaging inhibits this ability.

The paper's solution is **multi-head attention**: split the 512 dimensions into 8 pieces of 64 dimensions each (h = 8, dₖ = dᵥ = 64), give each piece its own W^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V} matrices to do attention independently, then concatenate the 8 results back to 512 dimensions and mix them with a matrix W^{O}. Because each head has one-eighth the dimensionality, the total computation is about the same as one full-size single head—so it is like getting seven extra experts for free.

formula.expr:
MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head₁, …, head₈) · W^{O}
headᵢ = Attention(Q·W_{i}^{Q}, K·W_{i}^{K}, V·W_{i}^{V})

parts.desc: Head i: use its own projection matrices to compress Q, K, V down to 64 dimensions, then run one scaled dot-product attention.
Concatenate the eight 64-dimensional outputs back to 8 × 64 = 512 dimensions.
Then multiply by a matrix to fuse the eight experts' opinions into one result.

fig.title: Two heads looking in different ways: head 1 tracks what “it” refers to, head 2 tracks the immediately preceding word
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers are examples, not from the paper. Each row is one word's attention distribution and sums to about 1; darker amber means more weight. The amber outline marks the row for “it.”
fig.note: Head 1: when reading “it,” most attention lands on “cat,” so the model can tell that “it” refers to the cat (the cat is hungry, not the mouse).

fig.title: Head 2 has a different pattern: almost every word attends to the word just before it
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers are examples, not from the paper.

blocks.p: This is not just a convenient story. The paper's appendix actually plots attention heads in a trained model: in layer 5 of the encoder, some heads reach across long distances, linking the verb “making” with the later words “more difficult”; two heads specialize in coreference, concentrating sharply on the word “Law” when reading “its”; other heads clearly follow sentence structure. The paper's conclusion: different heads really do learn different tasks.

fig.title: Too few or too many heads both hurt: 8 and 16 heads are best
fig.subtitle: Unit: BLEU on the English-to-German development set (newstest2013), with total computation held constant. Amber is the paper's default of 8 heads.
fig.note: From group (A) in Table 3 of the paper: more heads means fewer dimensions per head.

blocks.p: A single head scores 0.9 BLEU below the best setting; but more heads is not automatically better. At 32 heads each head has only 16 dimensions, too little capacity, and the score drops back to 25.4. 0.9 points may sound small, but remember the paper's record improvement was only about 2 points.

sections.h: No recurrence, so how does it know word order: positional encoding

blocks.p: Attention has a built-in blind spot: it **doesn't know order**. When each word looks at the whole sentence, it sees a set of words and their contents, with no information about which came first. If nothing is done, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look like the same three words to the model, and it can barely tell them apart. RNNs don't have this problem because they read in order by design; throw away recurrence, and you need another way to put order back.

The paper's solution is to create a “position vector” for each position and simply **add** it to the word embedding (both are 512-dimensional, so they can be summed). The position vectors are built from sine and cosine functions at different frequencies:

formula.expr:
PE(pos, 2i) = sin( pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}} )
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}} )

parts.desc: The word's position in the sentence: 0, 1, 2…
The dimension index: even dimensions use sin, odd dimensions use cos, paired two by two.
Controls the slowest wave: wavelengths stretch from 2π all the way to 10000·2π.

callout.title: Think of it as a clock with many hands.
callout.text: The second hand moves fast, the minute hand is slower, and the hour hand slower still. If you only look at the second hand, you cannot tell 1 o'clock from 2 o'clock; combine the positions of several hands and you can pin down a moment uniquely. The 512 dimensions of the positional encoding are like 256 pairs of hands running at different speeds—each pair has one sin and one cos—and every position gets a unique set of "hand readings."

blocks.p: Why sines and cosines specifically? The paper's reason: for any fixed offset k, the encoding for position pos+k can be written as a **linear function** of the encoding for position pos—the trigonometric angle-addition formulas guarantee this. That makes it easy for the model to learn relative position relationships such as "look three words ahead."

The paper also tried an alternative: skip the formula and let the model learn a vector for each position directly. The results were nearly identical (25.7 vs. 25.8 BLEU on the development set). The sinusoidal version was chosen because it may let the model handle sentences longer than anything seen in training, since the formula can produce an encoding for any position.

quiz.q: If you remove positional encoding entirely, what is the most direct capability the Transformer loses?
options: It cannot tell word order apart, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" become hard to distinguish.
It cannot process sentences longer than 512 tokens.
quiz.why: Attention itself is insensitive to order; word-order information comes entirely from positional encoding. Parallelism comes from the structure of attention, not from positional encoding, and multi-head attention still works fine—it just would not know who comes before whom.

sections.h: Putting the pieces together: 6 encoder layers, 6 decoder layers

blocks.p: Like the mainstream translation models of the time, the Transformer has two halves. The **encoder** reads the source text, such as an English sentence, and turns each word into a context-aware vector. The **decoder** takes those vectors and writes the translation, such as a German sentence, one word at a time; each time it writes a word, it feeds the words already written back in before writing the next. Both sides repeat the same layer structure 6 times (N = 6).

fig.title: Inside one encoder layer, a word passes through four steps
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: every step outputs 512-dimensional vectors, so they can be added together layer after layer.

steps.name: Multi-head self-attention
steps.desc: Each word looks at the whole sentence and mixes in information from other words according to how relevant they are.

steps.name: Residual + layer norm
steps.desc: Add this step's result back to the original input, then pull the values back into a stable range.

steps.name: Feed-forward network
steps.desc: Each word passes through a small two-layer network with ReLU in the middle, processing the information it has just gathered in place.

steps.name: Residual + layer norm
steps.desc: Again add back the input, normalize, and hand the result to the next layer.

parts.desc: Expand the 512-dimensional word vector to 2048 dimensions.
ReLU: negative values become 0, positive values stay unchanged, giving the network nonlinearity.
Then compress it back to 512 dimensions.

formula.note: Every position uses the same set of parameters, but different layers have different parameters. The paper notes you can also think of this as two convolutions with kernel size 1.

blocks.p: **Residual connection** means "copy the input unchanged and add it to the output." That way each layer only has to learn how much to change on top of what came in, and signals and gradients can travel through many layers along this shortcut, avoiding the problem of deep stacks becoming untrainable. It comes from ResNet in 2015, which the paper cites. **Layer normalization** pulls the values of each word vector back to roughly mean 0 and variance 1, making training more stable.
Each decoder layer has one more sub-layer than the encoder, three in total:

list: **Masked self-attention**: each word in the target sentence can only see itself and the words before it, not the ones after it. The implementation sets the scores for "future positions" to negative infinity before softmax, so those positions get zero weight afterward.

**Encoder–decoder attention**: the queries come from the decoder, and the keys and values come from the encoder's output. In other words, every time the model writes a German word, it looks back over the entire English source sentence.
**Feed-forward network**: the same as in the encoder.

callout.title: The mask is like covering up the answers during an exam
callout.text: During training, the entire correct translation is fed in at once, so all positions can be computed in parallel; but each position is masked from seeing what comes after it, so it can only predict the next word from the preceding words. This simulates the real "think as you write" generation process. Today's large language models generate text with this same mechanism.

callout.title: The Transformer is not only attention
callout.text: Using the paper's sizes, each layer has these parameters: the four attention projection matrices (W^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V}, W^{O}) add up to 4 × 512 × 512 parameters, and the feed-forward network has 2 × 512 × 2048. The latter is exactly twice the former, excluding biases. In other words, about two-thirds of the parameters in each layer sit in the feed-forward network. Attention moves information between words; the feed-forward network processes each word in place. Both are indispensable.

blocks.p: Two final design details: the input and output share the same word embedding matrix—the encoder embedding, decoder embedding, and the output layer that turns vectors back into words are one and the same—and the embeddings are multiplied by √d_{model} before the positional encoding is added.

sections.h: Why self-attention: the paper's three yardsticks

blocks.p: Section 4 of the paper directly answers "why self-attention" using three yardsticks: per-layer **computational complexity**, how parallelizable the layer is (measured by the minimum number of sequential steps required), and the **maximum path length** between any two positions. The comparison table earlier already gave the conclusion: self-attention connects any two words in a constant number of steps, the shortest path, and is also the most parallelizable.

Computational complexity deserves a closer look. Self-attention costs n²·d per layer—n words are compared pairwise, and each comparison has d dimensions—while a recurrent layer costs n·d². Which is cheaper depends on whether the sentence length n or the vector dimension d is larger:

fig.title: When sentences are shorter than the vector dimension, self-attention is cheaper; once they get long, it becomes far more expensive.
fig.subtitle: Illustrative estimate: d = 512, comparing only the order of magnitude of per-layer computation.

blocks.p: The paper points out that in the translation tasks of that time, sentences represented as subwords were usually much shorter than 512, so self-attention was faster. But it also clearly saw the downside: for very long sequences, each word could be restricted to attending only to a neighborhood of r words—restricted self-attention—at the cost of a maximum path length of O(n/r)—and it lists this as future work. That n² problem later became the core challenge for the whole "long context" research direction.
The paper also mentions a side benefit: attention weights can be inspected, making the model more interpretable. The "who is looking at whom" figures in the previous section are drawn this way.

quiz.q: According to the estimates above, when processing a long article of 4,000 subwords, self-attention's per-layer computation is roughly how many times the recurrent layer's?
quiz.why: The ratio of n²·d to n·d² is n / d = 4000 / 512 ≈ 7.8. Whenever the sequence length exceeds the vector dimension, self-attention becomes more expensive—and every time the length doubles, its computation quadruples.

sections.h: How it was trained: 8 GPUs, 12 hours to 3.5 days

list: **Data**: English-to-German used the WMT 2014 dataset, about 4.5 million sentence pairs, segmented into subwords with byte-pair encoding (BPE) using a shared vocabulary of about 37,000 subwords for English and German. English-to-French used a larger dataset of 36 million sentences with a vocabulary of 32,000 subwords. Each training batch contained roughly 25,000 source-language subwords and 25,000 target-language subwords.

**Hardware and duration**: one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model took about 0.4 seconds per step for 100,000 steps, totaling 12 hours; the big model took 1.0 second per step for 300,000 steps, totaling 3.5 days.

**Regularization**: dropout was applied to the output of each sub-layer before it was added back through the residual connection, with a rate of 0.1 for the base model; label smoothing was also set to 0.1.

blocks.p: The learning-rate schedule is carefully designed, and the paper gives a formula:

formula.expr: lrate = d_{model}^{−0.5} · min( step^{−0.5}, step · warmup^{−1.5} )

parts.desc: Which training step we are on
The number of warmup steps; the paper uses 4000

For the first 4000 steps, the second term dominates and the learning rate rises linearly with the step count; after that, the first term dominates and the learning rate declines slowly as the inverse square root of the step count.

callout.title: Why "warm up"?
callout.text: At the start of training the parameters are random, and the model has no idea which direction to go. Taking a big step right away makes it easy to stumble, with the loss swinging wildly or even diverging. So it starts with small steps, gradually accelerates, and once the direction stabilizes it slowly shortens its stride again. This "rise then fall" learning-rate curve later became close to standard practice for training Transformers.

callout.title: Label smoothing: deliberately making the model less confident
callout.text: During training, the model is not asked to give the correct answer a perfect score. Instead, it leaves a little probability for other words—the paper uses 0.1. The paper says this makes perplexity worse, because the model learns to be less certain, but final accuracy and BLEU both improve.

blocks.p: There are also a few techniques at test time: the base model averages the parameters from the last 5 checkpoints, and the big model averages the last 20. When generating translations, the model uses beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty α = 0.6, considering several candidate translations at once rather than picking only the best current word at each step.

sections.h: The report card: better, and far cheaper

callout.title: What is BLEU?
callout.text: The most common automatic benchmark for machine translation: it compares the model's output with a human reference translation and measures how many words and phrases overlap, on a scale of 0 to 100, higher being better. A gap of a few points is already considered a clear improvement in this field.

fig.title: English-to-German: the base Transformer beats every previous model, including ensembles
fig.subtitle: Unit: BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German test set (newstest2014). Amber marks the Transformer.
fig.note: From Table 2 of the paper. An ensemble combines the results of several models; it is usually stronger than a single model and also multiplies the cost.

fig.title: Training cost: the base Transformer used only a fraction of its rivals' compute
fig.subtitle: Unit: ×10¹⁸ floating-point operations, English-to-German. Amber marks the Transformer. The paper estimates this as training time × number of GPUs × per-GPU throughput.
fig.note: For example, 23 means 2.3×10¹⁹. The base model costs about one-third of ConvS2S yet scores more than 2 BLEU points higher.

blocks.p: On English-to-German, the big model reached 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 points above the previous best result—ConvS2S's ensemble score of 26.36. Even the base model, at 27.3, beat every published model and ensemble.

On English-to-French, the abstract and Table 2 report 41.8 BLEU, a new single-model record; but Section 6.1 of the body says 41.0. The two numbers are inconsistent, and the paper does not explain. It is worth noticing when reading, and it is better to cite the table as authoritative while mentioning the discrepancy. The paper also says its training cost was under one-quarter of the previous best model.

To show the Transformer is not just a translation model, the authors also applied it to **English constituency parsing**: the grammar tree of a sentence is written as a sequence of symbols, and the model is asked to "translate" into that. This task has output much longer than the input and strong structural constraints. Trained only on about 40,000 Wall Street Journal sentences, a 4-layer Transformer reached 91.3 F1; with extra semi-supervised data it reached 92.7, outperforming every previous method except a specially designed grammar model, RNNG at 93.3, with almost no task-specific tuning.

sections.h: Ablation experiments: which design choices really matter

blocks.p: Table 3 of the paper runs a set of controlled experiments: change one thing in the base model at a time and see how the English-to-German development score moves. This is the most reliable way to judge which design choices are actually essential.

fig.title: Change one thing at a time and see how the score moves
fig.subtitle: From Table 3 of the paper, English-to-German development set (newstest2013); the base model scores 25.8 BLEU with 65 million parameters. Blue columns show BLEU.
rows: Keys too short make it harder to judge how related two words are

blocks.p: Four conclusions can be drawn from this table. Multi-head attention clearly helps, but the number of heads should be moderate. A too-small dₖ hurts quality, and the paper infers that judging compatibility is not a simple job—perhaps a more complex match function than dot product would be better. Bigger models are better. And dropout is essential for avoiding overfitting.

callout.title: Learn to read an ablation table
callout.text: When a paper introduces several new designs at once, ablation experiments tell you how much each design contributes. When reading a paper, looking at the ablation table first is often more useful than the final headline numbers for judging where the paper's real contribution lies.

sections.h: What it did not solve, and the story after it

blocks.p: The paper ends by honestly listing what to do next, and those items happened to become the main threads of AI development in the following years:

list: **Long sequences are expensive**: self-attention's compute grows quadratically with sequence length. The paper suggests attending only to a local window; later sparse attention, efficient attention, and long-context techniques all grapple with this n².

**Generation is still sequential**: the decoder still writes one word at a time. The paper lists making generation less dependent on order as a research goal; today's large models still generate token by token, and inference acceleration remains a hot topic.

**Extending beyond text**: the paper plans to apply the Transformer to images, audio, and video. A few years later, Vision Transformer (2020) cut images into patches and read them like "words," and the diffusion model DiT (2022) also adopted the Transformer.

blocks.p: The Transformer's encoder and decoder were later split apart and developed separately: encoder-only BERT (2018) excels at understanding, while decoder-only GPT models excel at generation. Today's large language models mostly use only the decoder half, with refinements to normalization placement, positional encoding style, and other details—but the skeleton of "attention + feed-forward + residual connections" remains exactly the same as in this paper.

callout.title: What to read next
callout.text: These follow-up papers are all in our reading list: BERT, GPT-3, Vision Transformer, Scaling Laws, and more. We will unpack each one in depth, and completed close readings will appear on the paper page.

sections.h: Check yourself: have you really got it?

quiz.q: What is the most fundamental reason the Transformer can train much faster than an RNN?
options: All positions in a sentence can be computed at the same time, without waiting for the previous word
quiz.why: In an RNN, step t depends on the result of step t−1, so the computation has to queue up. In self-attention, every word looks directly at the whole sentence, and the whole sentence can be processed with matrix multiplication at once, making full use of GPU parallelism. The base model in the paper has 65 million parameters—not a small number.

quiz.q: In the decoder's encoder–decoder attention, where do the query (Q), key (K), and value (V) come from?
options: Q, K, and V all come from the encoder.
Q comes from the decoder; K and V come from the encoder output.
Q comes from the encoder; K and V come from the decoder.
Q, K, and V all come from the decoder.
quiz.why: The decoder uses its current state to ask the question (Q), then looks up the encoder's representation of the source sentence (K, V). This is the step where each written word looks back at the source sentence.

quiz.q: Why does the decoder's self-attention need a mask?
options: To prevent the model from peeking at the correct future answer when predicting a position
quiz.why: During training, the entire target sentence is fed in at once. Without masking later words, the model could read off the answer directly and never learn true word-by-word generation. The mask sets the scores for future positions to negative infinity, so their weights become 0 after softmax.
